Bedford
BED-furd
n. (the English county town of John Bunyan's congregation and of the gaol in which he spent twelve years and wrote)
From Old English, the ford of Beda, a personal name, with ford, a river crossing.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Bedford on the Ouse is the county town of Bedfordshire and the place of John Bunyan. Converted in the early sixteen-fifties and joined to the open-membership congregation gathered by John Gifford at Saint John's, he began preaching in 1655, was arrested in November 1660 under the restored Act of Uniformity for holding a meeting, and refused the condition of silence; he was held in the county gaol for twelve years to 1672 and again briefly in 1677. In prison he wrote Grace Abounding and began The Pilgrim's Progress, published in 1678, which has been translated into more languages than any English book but the Bible. He was afterwards pastor of the Bedford church until his death in 1688. The dictionary records Bedford because Bunyan's refusal was of a very specific kind: he was not asked to deny the faith, only to stop preaching, and he answered that if he were out today he would preach tomorrow.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a gaol as a prison; conformity as compliance with an established form; an allegory as a figurative discourse; a tinker as a mender of brass kettles; and a conventicle as a private religious assembly.

expand to see more

GAOL, n. A prison; a building or place for the confinement of debtors and criminals.

CONFORMITY, n. Correspondence with a model or pattern; compliance with the usages of the established church.

ALLEGORY, n. A figurative sentence or discourse, in which the principal subject is described by another subject resembling it in its properties and circumstances.

TINKER, n. A mender of brass kettles, pans and the like; an itinerant mender of household vessels.

CONVENTICLE, n. An assembly for religious worship; appropriately, an assembly of dissenters, so called in contempt.

Modern Corruption

English county town of Bunyan's open-membership congregation and of the gaol where he spent twelve years and began The Pilgrim's Progress.

expand to see more

The corruption to name is the law that permits a man his belief and forbids him his voice, which is the exact shape of the Act under which Bunyan was held. He was never required to recant; he was required to be quiet, and the dictionary insists that this is not a lesser demand. Peter and John gave the only possible answer to it: “For we cannot but speak the things which we have seen and heard” (Act 4:20), and the apostles' practice under prohibition was simply to continue, for “daily in the temple, and in every house, they ceased not to teach and preach Jesus Christ” (Act 5:42).

The second paragraph names the principle to recover, which is what God does with a prison. Paul found that his confinement served the thing it was meant to stop, “the things which happened unto me have fallen out rather unto the furtherance of the gospel” (Php 1:12). Hebrews lists imprisonment among the honours of faith rather than its interruptions, naming those who “had trial of cruel mockings and scourgings, yea, moreover of bonds and imprisonment” (Heb 11:36). The dictionary observes that twelve years in Bedford gaol produced the most widely read book in the English language after the Bible, and that no plan of Bunyan's could have arranged it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek parresia (G3954), boldness of speech; Greek prokope (G4297), furtherance; Greek desmos (G1199), a bond.

expand to see more

Greek laleo (G2980) — to speak, to utter; “For we cannot but speak the things which we have seen and heard”, Acts 4:20.

Greek pauo (G3973) — to cease, to stop; “they ceased not to teach and preach Jesus Christ”, Acts 5:42.

Greek prokope (G4297) — progress, furtherance; “unto the furtherance of the gospel”, Philippians 1:12.

Greek desmos (G1199) — a band, a bond, imprisonment; “of bonds and imprisonment”, Hebrews 11:36.

Greek empaigmos (G1701) — mockery, derision; “had trial of cruel mockings and scourgings”, Hebrews 11:36.

Usage

"“For we cannot but speak the things which we have seen and heard” (Act 4:20) — the only answer to an order of silence."

"“they ceased not to teach and preach Jesus Christ” (Act 5:42) — the apostolic practice under prohibition."

"“unto the furtherance of the gospel” (Php 1:12) — what God does with a prison."
